chapterTitle: Have Your Feelings (Or They Will Have You)
provenanceNote: All content original paraphrase. No verbatim text from published book. All scenarios invented fresh.

frameworks.definition: Suppressed feelings do not disappear. They redirect into tone, contempt, avoidance, and sudden escalation. The feelings conversation is already happening; the question is whether it is happening above or below ground.

The chapter's moves are to find what you are actually feeling, negotiate with your feelings by inspecting the story beneath them, not let feelings drive the conversation, share feelings directly, and acknowledge the other person's feelings before trying to solve anything.
A direct feelings statement reports what is happening inside you. A feelings-shaped accusation disguises a verdict about the other person as if it were a feeling statement.

The cost of emotional expression is not evenly distributed. In some contexts the feelings conversation still needs to happen, but with a safer audience or channel than the person the feelings are about.

anchors.label: Shelved project meeting
anchors.description: Tara asks for a meeting to understand the business reasoning behind shelving a project, but the real underground feelings are grief, fear, and anger.
anchors.friction: A facts conversation cannot satisfy the real need because the actual conversation is about the emotional impact of the decision.
anchors.consequence: The meeting leaves both people more frustrated and neither understands why.

anchors.label: Performed cheerfulness in a friend group
anchors.description: Rourke has been performing cheerfulness around Zoe for months after feeling dismissed at a group dinner.
anchors.friction: The performance is visible to everyone else and changes how the group behaves, even though Rourke keeps insisting it is not worth raising.
anchors.consequence: The group splits quietly around an unspoken feeling that keeps leaking anyway.

anchors.label: I'm fine in a 1:1
anchors.description: Sadie tells Ben she is fine when she is not, and Ben politely accepts it even though both feel worse by the end of the meeting.
anchors.friction: Both perform normalcy instead of leaving space for the actual emotional situation.
anchors.consequence: The work problem continues until it becomes harder to address helpfully.

limits: Sharing feelings is not always the right move with the person the feelings are about; some contexts require a safer audience or different channel.
Acknowledging the other person's feelings does not mean agreeing with the story producing those feelings.
Power, role, and stereotype pressures can make the cost of expressing feelings very unequal across contexts.
